title: Post-operative surgical menopause and HRT discussion

header.contentArea: Managing surgical menopause in a BRCA carrier with a breast cancer history
guidelineVersions: NICE CG164: Familial breast cancer (Published June 2013; last updated November 2023)
NICE NG101: Early and locally advanced breast cancer (Published 18 July 2018; last updated 14 April 2025)
RCOG Scientific Impact Paper No. 66 (1st edition, January 2023)
British Menopause Society: Tool for Clinicians — Surgical Menopause (September 2024)

related.why: The surgery that has caused this surgical menopause
The earlier discussion where this trade-off was first raised

brief.setting: Post-operative follow-up clinic, four weeks after surgery
brief.role: Core surgical trainee, supporting the multidisciplinary follow-up
brief.scenario: Ms Linford, 44, is four weeks after risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and reports significant hot flushes and low mood, and asks about hormone replacement therapy.
brief.task: Discuss her symptoms and the options for managing them, given her breast cancer history. You have 7 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Acknowledge the impact of her symptoms, be honest about the complexity of HRT given her ER-positive cancer history, and offer both hormonal and non-hormonal avenues without dismissing her request.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Refusing to discuss HRT outright because of her cancer history, rather than explaining the actual balance of considerations and referring appropriately.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Tell me more about how these symptoms have been affecting you day to day."

flow: Explore the impact of her symptoms
Explain the general principles around HRT and hormone-sensitive cancer
Discuss the possibility of specialist review for HRT

grid.label: Exploring symptom impact
grid.fail: Moves straight to management without asking how symptoms are actually affecting her.
grid.pass: Asks about the nature and impact of her symptoms (e.g. frequency of flushes, sleep, mood, daily function) before discussing management.
grid.high: Explicitly validates that surgical menopause can be more sudden and intense than natural menopause, rather than treating her symptoms as routine.

grid.label: Explaining the HRT complexity
grid.fail: Gives a blanket "no" or "yes" to HRT without explaining why it's more complex given her history.
grid.pass: Explains that HRT is generally more complex to consider in someone with a history of ER-positive breast cancer, and needs specialist input to weigh benefits and risks.
grid.high: Explains this without shutting down her question, framing it as a decision that deserves proper specialist assessment rather than a quick answer.

grid.label: Non-hormonal options
grid.fail: Offers no alternative if HRT isn't straightforward.
grid.pass: Mentions non-hormonal options for menopausal symptoms, such as certain non-hormonal medications and lifestyle measures.
grid.high: Tailors the discussion to which of her symptoms (flushes vs mood) might respond to which options, rather than a generic list.

grid.label: Referral for specialist input
grid.fail: Does not offer any pathway to a more detailed HRT discussion.
grid.pass: Offers referral to an appropriate specialist (e.g. oncology or menopause specialist) to weigh up HRT in detail given her specific cancer history.
grid.high: Explains this referral will look at the full picture, including her cancer type and how long ago it was, rather than applying a blanket rule.

grid.label: Addressing low mood
grid.fail: Attributes low mood entirely to hormones without further exploration.
grid.pass: Asks further about her low mood specifically, rather than assuming it is only hormonal.
grid.high: Checks for broader wellbeing given her cumulative experience this year, and signposts to psychological support if appropriate, without diagnosing her.

grid.label: Closing and follow-up
grid.fail: Ends without a clear plan or follow-up.
grid.pass: Summarises the plan (referral, non-hormonal options to try in the meantime) and arranges follow-up.
grid.high: Checks she feels her concerns have been taken seriously before closing.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: The hot flushes are awful, and I've been feeling really low. Can I have HRT?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, you can't have HRT, you've had breast cancer.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: There's not really anything else I can offer, I'm afraid.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Tell me more about how these symptoms have been affecting you day to day.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: The flushes wake me up most nights, and I've just felt really flat since the surgery.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That sounds exhausting, and surgical menopause can hit harder and faster than the natural kind. On HRT - given your history of ER-positive breast cancer, it's more complicated than a simple yes or no, and needs specialist input to weigh up properly.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Is there anything else that could help in the meantime?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes - there are non-hormonal medications that can help with hot flushes, and some lifestyle measures too, which we can start now.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll refer you to the menopause specialist team to properly weigh up HRT given your specific history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: On the low mood - is that mainly linked to the flushes and poor sleep, or is it more than that?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Probably a bit of both, if I'm honest.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That makes sense given everything this year - let's start the non-hormonal options and the referral, and review how you're doing at follow-up.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Tell me more about how these symptoms have been affecting your day to day, and your sleep and mood specifically.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: The flushes are constant and wake me most nights, and I just feel flat and tearful a lot of the time.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's a genuinely hard combination, and I want to say - surgical menopause can be far more sudden and intense than the natural kind, so what you're feeling isn't unusual or something to just push through.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Can I have hormone replacement therapy?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's a fair question to ask, and I don't want to just say no - HRT after ER-positive breast cancer is genuinely more complex, since hormones can be relevant to that type of cancer, so it needs a specialist to weigh your specific situation properly, rather than a blanket answer from me today.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In the meantime, there are non-hormonal medications that can help with the flushes specifically, and some approaches like CBT or exercise that can help with both flushes and mood.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll refer you to the menopause specialist team, who'll look at your full picture, including your cancer type and timeline, rather than a one-size-fits-all rule.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: On the low mood - is that mostly tied to the flushes and poor sleep, or does it feel bigger than that, given everything you've been through this year?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Honestly, it feels bigger than just the flushes.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Thank you for being honest about that - I'd like to make sure you have support for that too, alongside the physical symptoms, and we'll bring all of this together at your follow-up.

failures.move: Giving a flat "no" to HRT without explanation or referral.
failures.consequence: Dismisses a legitimate question and denies her access to a properly weighed specialist opinion that could still lead to HRT in some circumstances.

failures.move: Attributing low mood entirely to hormones without further exploration.
failures.consequence: Risks missing a broader wellbeing need that deserves its own attention, separate from the physical menopause symptoms.

failures.move: Offering no alternative when HRT isn't straightforward.
failures.consequence: Leaves her without any options for genuinely distressing symptoms in the interim.

failures.move: Ending the consultation with no summary or follow-up plan after declining to help further.
failures.consequence: She leaves without any plan, referral or safety-net despite highly distressing, unresolved symptoms.

recovery.when: You gave a flat no to HRT
recovery.line: I shouldn't have just said no - let me explain why it's more complicated, and how we can get you a proper specialist opinion.

recovery.when: You assumed her low mood was only hormonal
recovery.line: Let me ask a bit more - does this feel like just the flushes and sleep, or something wider?

knowledge.fact: HRT after a diagnosis of ER-positive breast cancer requires careful, individualised specialist assessment rather than a blanket rule, given the hormone-sensitive nature of the cancer.
Non-hormonal options, including certain medications and lifestyle or psychological approaches, can help manage menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes when HRT is not straightforward.
Surgical menopause following bilateral oophorectomy tends to cause more sudden and severe symptoms than natural menopause.

recall.think: Don't dismiss the HRT question; explain complexity; offer non-hormonal help; low mood may not be hormonal.
recall.say: "It's a fair question to ask, and I don't want to just say no."
do: Explore symptom impact, including low mood, first
Explain HRT needs specialist input given her ER-positive history

numbers.meaning: age HRT is usually advisable to, without breast cancer; her ER-positive history needs individual assessment

recall.trap: Refusing HRT outright, or assuming low mood is only hormonal.
recall.finish: Specialist HRT referral, non-hormonal options started, low mood explored.

sources.name: NICE CG164: Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer
sources.supports: Assessing likelihood of an inherited breast cancer predisposition, referral for genetic testing, implications of a pathogenic variant for the patient and relatives, and that first-degree relatives of a carrier have up to a 50% chance of carrying the same variant

sources.name: RCOG Scientific Impact Paper No. 66: Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy and the use of hormone replacement therapy below the age of natural menopause
sources.supports: HRT is usually advisable up to age 51 for women undergoing early or surgical menopause who have not had breast cancer; for a history of receptor-negative breast cancer, gynaecology liaises with oncology case-by-case; no blanket recommendation is given for ER-positive disease, reflecting the need for individualised specialist assessment

sources.name: British Menopause Society: Tool for Clinicians — Surgical Menopause
sources.supports: Surgical menopause causes a sudden, complete loss of ovarian hormone production and can produce more severe symptoms than gradual natural menopause; women with both an increased ovarian cancer risk and a personal history of breast cancer should discuss HRT with their breast cancer team before starting it; non-hormonal options include SSRIs, clonidine, gabapentin, fezolinetant and cognitive behavioural therapy

partner.opening: This patient is four weeks post-oophorectomy with menopausal symptoms and a question about HRT. You have 7 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 44, four weeks after surgery, with severe hot flushes disrupting sleep and a persistent low mood you suspect is more than just hormonal. You want to ask about HRT but worry you'll simply be told no because of your cancer history.

reveals.trigger: Candidate explores the impact of your symptoms in detail
reveals.finding: You describe disrupted sleep and low mood, feeling more comfortable being open.

reveals.trigger: Candidate explains the HRT complexity rather than a flat refusal
reveals.finding: You feel taken seriously rather than dismissed.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks whether your low mood is more than just the physical symptoms
reveals.finding: You admit it feels bigger than just the flushes.

push.question: Can I have HRT or not?
push.expect: Explain this needs specialist assessment given her ER-positive history, rather than a simple yes or no, and arrange that referral.

push.question: Is there anything that can help until I see a specialist?
push.expect: Offer non-hormonal options for symptom relief in the meantime.

curveballs.prompt: I feel like no one is taking my mood seriously, they just talk about the hot flushes.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge this directly, apologise for any sense of that, and ensure her low mood is addressed as its own concern alongside the physical symptoms.

curveballs.prompt: What if the specialist also says no to HRT?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge that's possible, but explain the assessment considers her individual case properly, and non-hormonal options remain available regardless of the outcome.
